question_text: Why is Public Private Partnership (PPP) required in infrastructural projects? Examine the role of PPP model in the redevelopment of Railway Stations in India. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: The state needs capital and a builder faster than the budget allows
PPP shares the money and also the risk
A station is a transport node and a commercial site together
The model works only if the public purpose stays in the contract

points.text: Infrastructure needs more capital and speed than the public budget alone can give, which is why PPP is used.
A private partner brings money, a construction discipline and a use of the commercial space.
Railway stations are being bid as a station plus shops, offices and a passenger facility, so the commercial rent pays part of the public work.
The risk is a pretty mall and a poor platform. The contract has to lock passenger amenity, a fare and a takeover if the partner fails.
PPP is required for the scale. At a station it is justified only if the passenger, not the shop, remains the purpose.

question_text: Is inclusive growth possible under market economy? State the significance of financial inclusion in achieving economic growth in India. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: A market grows; it does not by itself include
Inclusion is possible if the rules reach the last person
A bank account, credit and insurance are how the poor enter the market
Financial inclusion is a means of growth, not a side scheme

points.text: Inclusive growth is possible in a market economy, but only if the market is opened to people it currently ignores.
A pure market rewards whoever already has land, a firm or a degree.
Financial inclusion — an account, a small credit, a pension, an insurance — lets a household save, borrow for a tool and survive a shock.
In India that access has widened the base of consumption and of tiny enterprise, which is itself growth.
The market can include. Financial inclusion is one of the doors through which it does.

question_text: What are the major challenges of Public Distribution System (PDS) in India? How can it be made effective and transparent? (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Leakage, a wrong list and a thin nutrition are the old challenges
A digital pipe reduces the ghost and can exclude the real
Effectiveness is grain that arrives, of a quality people will eat
Transparency is a list and a stock the public can see

points.text: The PDS still loses grain, misses people and sometimes offers what people will not lift.
Inclusion and exclusion errors, diversion, and a diet of only rice and wheat are the core challenges.
Portability, an online stock and a social audit make diversion harder.
Adding pulses and an oil, a local grievance that actually restores a name, and a dealer the panchayat can see, make it both effective and transparent.
The fix is a correct list, a visible stock and a food basket wider than a cereal.

question_text: Elaborate the scope and significance of the food processing industry in India. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: India produces a lot and processes little
Processing cuts the waste between the field and the town
It is a rural job and a farmer's price, not only a factory
The scope runs from a pack shed to an export brand

points.text: Food processing is the missing industry between India's harvest and India's market.
Sorting, cold storage, milling, dairy and a ready food reduce the share of the crop that rots.
The job is near the farm, so it matters for a rural wage and for a woman worker.
A processed good also earns more in an export and in a city than the raw crop.
Its significance is that it turns a surplus that spoils into an income that lasts.

question_text: The increase in life expectancy in the country has led to newer health challenges in the community. What are those challenges and what steps need to be taken to meet them? (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: People live longer, so chronic disease replaces the old infectious peak
An ageing parent needs care the joint family no longer fully gives
The health system is still built for a short illness
The step is primary care, a geriatric service and a way to pay for a long illness

points.text: Longer life has shifted the health burden from a short infection to a long condition.
Diabetes, heart disease, cancer and a failing joint now dominate, along with the mental health of the old.
Households face a cost that lasts years, and women carry the unpaid care.
The response is a primary clinic that follows a chronic patient, a geriatric ward, a health cover that includes outpatient care, and prevention in diet and activity.
The new challenge is not how to survive childhood. It is how to live the extra years without being ruined by them.

question_text: Each year a large amount of plant material, cellulose, is deposited on the surface of Planet Earth. What are the natural processes this cellulose undergoes before yielding carbon dioxide, water and other end products? (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: Cellulose is a tough chain of glucose
Microbes, not a simple fire, do most of the work
Enzymes cut the chain, then respiration finishes it
The end products are carbon dioxide, water and a humus

points.text: Fallen plant cellulose is broken down by living decomposers, step by step.
Fungi and bacteria secrete cellulase, which cuts the long chain into shorter sugars.
Those sugars are then respired. In air this yields carbon dioxide and water. In a waterlogged, airless soil it can yield methane as well.
Part of the material is left as humus, which holds the soil, and the minerals return to the cycle.
The natural process is enzymatic decay followed by microbial respiration.

question_text: Discuss in detail the photochemical smog emphasizing its formation, effects and mitigation. Explain the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Photochemical smog and the Gothenburg Protocol
topics: Photochemical smog and the Gothenburg Protocol
keyPointers: This smog is made by sunlight acting on vehicle and industrial fumes
Nitrogen oxides and volatile organics produce ozone near the ground
It burns lungs, crops and a material
Gothenburg is the international agreement aimed at the gases that cause it

points.text: Photochemical smog forms when sunlight cooks nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds into ozone and other irritants.
Vehicles, a refinery and a solvent are the sources. The brown haze, a chest illness and a damaged crop are the effects.
Mitigation is a cleaner vehicle, a vapour control, a public transport and a limit on the precursor gases.
The 1999 Gothenburg Protocol, under the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, sets national ceilings on those pollutants, including the ones that make ozone.
The Protocol matters because the gas that makes the smog does not stop at a city boundary.

question_text: Explain the mechanism and occurrence of cloudburst in the context of the Indian subcontinent. Discuss two recent examples. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: A cloudburst is an extreme rain in a very small area in a very short time
Moist monsoon air forced up a steep slope can do it
The Himalaya and the Western Ghats are the usual sites
The harm is a flash flood, because the slope cannot hold the water

points.text: A cloudburst occurs when a saturated column is lifted suddenly and drops its water on one valley.
Orographic lift along the Himalaya or the Ghats, a convective tower and a slow-moving storm are the mechanism.
They occur in the monsoon, often in the afternoon or night, over a few square kilometres.
Recent Indian examples include the cloudbursts over Uttarakhand and Himachal valleys, and events around Leh and Amarnath, each followed by a flash flood and a landslide.
The subcontinent's steep, wet margins are where this mechanism keeps recurring.

question_text: Discuss the types of organised crimes. Describe the linkages between terrorists and organised crime that exist at the national and transnational levels. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Organised crime and its link with terror
topics: Organised crime and its link with terror
keyPointers: Organised crime is a continuing enterprise, not a one-off offence
Drugs, arms, trafficking, extortion and a cyber fraud are the types
Terror borrows the crime's route, money and document
The link is national and, through a border and a bank, transnational

points.text: Organised crime is a structured group that lives off a repeated illegal market.
Drug trafficking, arms, human trafficking, extortion, counterfeit currency and cyber fraud are the main types.
A terrorist group uses the same hawala, the same tunnel and the same forged paper. In return the criminal buys protection or a cause's cover.
Inside India the link shows in a fake note, a drug route and an extortion racket. Across borders it shows in arms, narcotics and a sanctuary.
The linkage is an exchange: the crime supplies logistics, the terror supplies intimidation and a purpose.

question_text: What are the maritime security challenges in India? Discuss the organisational, technical and procedural initiatives taken to improve the maritime security. (Answer in 150 words)
keyPointers: The challenge is a long coast, a busy sea lane and a thin watch
Terror from the sea, piracy, trafficking and a grey-zone intrusion are the threats
India answered with a clearer command and a coastal chain of radars
Organisation, technology and a procedure had all been missing in 2008

points.text: India's maritime security problem is the size of the sea it must watch.
A terror landing, piracy on the sea lanes, trafficking, illegal fishing and a neighbour's survey ship are the challenges.
After 2008 the Navy was given the lead, a coastal police and a new coastal command were built, and fishing boats were registered.
Radars, an automatic identification system and joint procedures for who boards a boat closed the gaps between agencies.
The initiatives work only if the organisation, the sensor and the procedure stay joined.

question_text: “Economic growth in the recent past has been led by increase in labour productivity.” Explain this statement. Suggest the growth pattern that will lead to creation of more jobs without compromising labour productivity. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Recent growth came from each worker producing more, not from many more workers
A rising productivity with flat employment is a jobless pattern
The answer is not to make labour less productive
It is to spread the productive work into more firms and more sectors

points.text: The statement means that output rose because output per worker rose, while the number of good jobs did not rise in step.
Services and a capital-intensive plant delivered the productivity. Construction and a small firm absorbed people at low productivity.
Breaking productivity to 'create' jobs would only create poor jobs.
A better pattern raises productivity in the labour-using sectors: a labour-intensive manufacture, a food processing unit, a care and a logistics job that uses a better tool.
Skills, a small-firm credit and a demand for these goods let productivity and headcount rise together.
The growth to want is one where more workers are pulled into already rising productivity, not one where productivity is sacrificed.

question_text: Do you think India will meet 50 percent of its energy needs from renewable energy by 2030? Justify your answer. How will the shift of subsidies from fossil fuels to renewables help achieve the above objective? Explain. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: A 50 percent renewable target and subsidies
topics: A 50 percent renewable target and subsidies
keyPointers: The 50 percent figure is about installed capacity, and the question says energy needs
Capacity is achievable; a half of all energy used is much harder
Coal still anchors the night and the industry
Moving the subsidy changes which plant gets built

points.text: India can approach a very high renewable share of new electricity capacity. Meeting half of all energy needs by 2030 is a harder claim, and on present trends it is unlikely without a faster shift.
Electricity is only part of energy. Transport, cooking and industry still burn fossil fuels.
Solar and wind are now cheap when the sun and the wind are there, and weak when they are not. Storage and a grid decide the real share.
A subsidy on a fossil fuel pays people to keep the old plant. Shifting it to storage, a rooftop and a green industry lowers the renewable's cost and raises the fossil plant's.
That shift helps the objective. It does not, by itself, replace the fuel outside the power sector by 2030.
The subsidy shift is necessary. The 50 percent of energy needs is not yet secured by it.

question_text: What are the main bottlenecks in upstream and downstream process of marketing of agricultural products in India? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Upstream is everything before the produce is assembled
Downstream is everything after it leaves the farmer's gate
Both ends leak value, for different reasons
The farmer meets the bottleneck as a low price and a rejected lot

points.text: Farm marketing is blocked before the crop is gathered and again before it reaches the eater.
Upstream: small and scattered holdings, weak grading, little storage on the farm, a tenancy that discourages investment, and a price signal that arrives too late to change what is sown.
Downstream: too many hands between the mandi and the retail shelf, a cold chain that breaks, a law and a fee that fragment the market, and a processor who will not buy an uneven lot.
Roads, a packhouse and a contract that is actually enforced sit on the boundary of the two.
The result is waste, a high retail price and a low farm price at the same time.
The bottleneck is not one market. It is the missing link on both sides of the farmer.

question_text: What is Integrated Farming System? How is it helpful to small and marginal farmers in India? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Integrated farming joins crop, animal, fish and a tree on one small holding
The waste of one part is the input of the next
A small farmer gains income in more months, and a shock hits only one part
It uses the family's labour, which is the resource they have

points.text: An integrated farming system is a planned mix of enterprises on the same farm so that each feeds another.
A crop's residue feeds a cow. The cow's waste feeds a biogas plant and a fish pond. A tree on the bund gives fruit and fuel.
For a small and marginal farmer the mix means some receipt in a month when the field crop pays nothing.
Bought inputs fall because the farm recycles them. Risk falls because a failed rain does not destroy the hen and the pond together.
It fits a holding that cannot live on one crop's surplus.
It helps precisely the farmer who is too small for a single specialised enterprise.

question_text: Launched on 25th December, 2021, James Webb Space Telescope has been much in the news since then. What are its unique features which make it superior to its predecessor Space Telescopes? What are the key goals of this mission? What potential benefits does it hold for the human race? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: Webb sees in the infrared, from a point far beyond Earth's heat
A gold mirror and a sunshield are what make that possible
The goals are the first galaxies, a star being born and a planet's atmosphere
The benefit is knowledge, and the technology spun off to reach it

points.text: James Webb is superior because it observes a light its predecessors could not, from a place they did not sit.
A large segmented mirror, a fold-out sunshield and a station at a Lagrange point keep the instruments cold enough for infrared.
Hubble's strength was visible and ultraviolet light from low Earth orbit. Webb looks through dust and far back in time.
The goals are the earliest galaxies, how stars and planets form, and the chemistry of atmospheres that might hold the conditions for life.
For the human race the gain is a deeper origin story, and the materials, optics and a cryogenic engineering built to get it.
The mission's benefit is a better answer to where the universe, and possibly life, came from.

question_text: What is the basic principle behind vaccine development? How do vaccines work? What approaches were adopted by the Indian vaccine manufacturers to produce COVID-19 vaccines? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece of the pathogen
Memory cells then answer the real infection faster
India used more than one platform for COVID-19
A whole inactivated virus and a viral vector were the two large Indian routes

points.text: A vaccine works by teaching immunity in advance, without causing the disease.
The principle is to present an antigen — a killed germ, a weakened one, a protein or the gene for a protein — so that antibodies and T cells are made and remembered.
On a later exposure those memory cells respond before the pathogen can spread.
Indian manufacturers used an inactivated whole virus for Covaxin, and a viral-vector carrying the spike gene for Covishield, produced at a scale the country could fill into vials.
Other platforms, including a protein subunit and later an mRNA effort, were also pursued.
The approaches differed in how they delivered the spike. The principle, an immune memory, was the same.

question_text: Discuss global warming and mention its effects on the global climate. Explain the control measures to bring down the level of greenhouse gases which cause global warming, in the light of the Kyoto Protocol, 1997. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Global warming and the Kyoto Protocol
topics: Global warming and the Kyoto Protocol
keyPointers: Warming is the rise in temperature from gases that trap heat
The climate answer is a hotter extreme, a higher sea and a shifted rain
Control means emitting less and taking some back
Kyoto was the first treaty that set binding cuts on developed countries

points.text: Global warming is the rise in the Earth's average temperature as greenhouse gases hold back outgoing heat.
Effects include hotter extremes, a melting ice, a rising sea, a stronger rain in some places and a longer drought in others, and a stress on a crop and a species.
Control is energy efficiency, a shift off coal, a stop to deforestation, and a sink in a forest and a soil.

The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 required listed developed countries to cut their emissions against a 1990 base, and invented trading, joint implementation and a clean development mechanism so a cut could be made where it was cheaper.
It did not bind the large emerging emitters, which limited its reach, but it established that a cut can be a legal duty.
Kyoto's lesson is a binding target plus a flexible way to meet it.

question_text: Explain the causes and effects of coastal erosion in India. What are the available coastal management techniques for combating the hazard? (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: The sea, a dam and a bad wall all move sand
The east coast and some western stretches lose the beach
The effect is a lost house, a salinised field and a weaker storm defence
Management is a mix of holding the line and giving the beach room

points.text: Coastal erosion in India is the net loss of beach and dune under waves, a reduced supply of sand, and human structures.
Dams trap the river sand that used to feed the coast. A port and a seawall then starve the down-drift beach. A rising sea and a cyclone accelerate the loss, especially on the sandy east coast.
Villages, a road and a farmland fall in. Salt enters wells. The natural buffer against the next storm thins.
Techniques include a beach nourishment, a dune planted with vegetation, a groyne or an offshore reef used carefully, and a setback that does not build on the line that will go.
Hard walls alone often shift the erosion to the next village.
The better management gives the coast sediment and space, and uses a wall only where a town cannot move.

question_text: What are the different elements of cyber security? Keeping in view the challenges in cyber security, examine the extent to which India has successfully developed a comprehensive National Cyber Security Strategy. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Elements of cyber security and India's strategy
topics: Elements of cyber security and India's strategy
keyPointers: Cyber security is confidentiality, integrity and availability, plus the people and the law around them
The challenge is a weak device, a critical system and a cross-border attacker
India has built agencies, a law and a sectoral defence
A single written national strategy has lagged the threat

points.text: The elements of cyber security are a protected network, a trustworthy data, a system that stays up, and a user who does not open the door.
Add identity, a response when the breach happens, and a law that can reach the offender.
India's challenges are a huge number of first-time users, old software in a critical sector, and attackers based abroad.
CERT-In, a national critical-information protection centre, the IT Act and sectoral rules for a bank and a power grid are a real architecture.
What has been slower is one comprehensive, public, updated national strategy that joins the military, the civilian and the state cyber units under a single plan.
India has built many of the pieces. The comprehensive strategy is still more a set of institutions than a finished document.

question_text: Naxalism is a social, economic and developmental issue manifesting as a violent internal security threat. In this context, discuss the emerging issues and suggest a multilayered strategy to tackle the menace of Naxalism. (Answer in 250 words)
keyPointers: The violence sits on a real grievance of land, forest and a missing state
Emerging issues include a smaller area, a better-armed core and a development the cadre tries to block
Security without a right, or a scheme without security, each fails
The strategy has to be several layers at once

points.text: Naxalism is a development failure that has taken the form of an armed organisation.

Emerging issues: the affected area has shrunk but the remaining zones are denser; a road and a mobile tower are both a gain and a target; mining and a forest right collide; urban support networks persist.

A multilayered strategy holds the security layer (a local force, intelligence, and justice for a surrendered cadre), the rights layer (forest rights, a land record, a quick court), and the development layer (a school, a health post and a job that the state, not the cadre, delivers).
A fourth layer is political: a panchayat that actually functions, so the armed group is not the only authority.
Excess of force without the other layers recruits the next cadre.
The menace recedes when the state is present as both a protector and a provider.
